figures.caption_snippet: Figure 1: Performance results on BrowseComp-zh (avg) and WideSearch (avg/max).

Figure 2: Overview of the InfoSeeker framework. The system features a three-tier topology consisting of a strategic Host, domain-specific Managers, and tool-executing Workers. By enforcing hierarchical context isolation, high-level directives (qt) are decomposed into parallelisable subtasks (qk t ) by Managers and executed by Workers. Final results are aggregated into concise summaries (yt) to support long-horizon planning while preventing context exhaustion at the strategic level.
Figure 3: Time efficiency comparison. InfoSeeker achieves a more than 2× reduction in inference time, enabled by its efficient parallelism design.
Figure 4: The Impact of Worker Pool Size. End-to-end inference time vs. worker-pool size. Larger pools reduce latency by enabling concurrent execution of weakly coupled subtasks.
Figure 5: Execution trace: Michelin three-star restaurant synthesis.
Figure 6 presents a historical riddle reasoning example from BrowseComp-zh that showcases multi-manager collabora- tion between search and browser agents.

Figure 7 illustrates a failure case from BrowseComp-zh on disease name identification, where an answer-type mismatch causes the system to return a plausible disease class instead of the required canonical entity. This error arises from misinterpreting subtype cues under uncertainty, revealing a limitation in entity-level constraint handling.

Figure 8 illustrates a failure case from WideSearch on comprehensive data aggregation, where context length constraints compel the system to return a representative sample instead of the requested exhaustive list. This error arises from a token overflow during the processing of high-volume retrieval results, revealing a fundamental scalability bottleneck in large-scale information synthesis.

Figure 1: Spider plot demonstrating the relative performance of all evaluated approaches on three different environments – SMACv2, Google Research Football (GRF) and POGEMA.

Figure 2: The general pipeline begins with training expert policies across diverse MARL environments using domain-appropriate algorithms (e.g., IPPO, RHCR). These policies generate large-scale datasets of observation-action(-reward) trajectories. MARL- GPT is then trained on the aggregated data using cross-entropy loss to predict expert actions and Q-values, enabling a single model to generalize across environments, tasks, and coordination regimes.

Figure 3: Illustration of the proposed encoding scheme for multi-agent systems, demonstrated using an example from the SMACv2 environment. Each agent receives a structured, vectorized observation containing information about itself, its allies, and nearby enemies. Figure 5: Modular and reconfigurable maze environment composed of standardized floor and wall units.
Figure 6: Waveshare JetBot robotic agent used for maze navi- gation experiments.
Figure 7: Real-world execution of a scenario based on maze scenario with 3 robots. Left: simulated environment in POGEMA. Right: corresponding physical setup used for real- world deployment.

Figure 2: Pass^3 rate by difficulty level. All models degrade from Easy to Hard.

Figure 3: Comparison of a vanilla LLM judge against the hybrid grading pipeline across five models. The vanilla judge receives the full conversation transcript and complete grader source code; only server-side audit logs and post-execution environment snapshots are withheld.
Figure 4: Effect of error injection on agent performance. Three models are evaluated on General tasks at error rates 0.0–0.6. Pass@3 remains largely stable while Pass^3 drops sharply.
